prompt:
I present to our board on Thursday and I have 15 minutes. Two of the five board members aren't in food at all. Can you put the deck together for me, including what I should say? Here's everything I have:

- Hollis & Rye runs 11 cafes, supplied by two commissary kitchens (Eastside and Mill Street)
- Weekday utilization: Eastside 94%, Mill Street 81%
- We plan 3 new cafes over the next 14 months, which means we need about 30% more output by next fall
- In the last two quarters we turned down 17 wholesale orders, roughly $210,000 in revenue
- Option A: lease the Dunmore site. Rent quoted at $9,400 a month, build-out estimate $610,000, about 9 months until it can produce
- Option B: add a second shift at Eastside. About $180,000 a year in added labor, and it tops out around +26% output
- What I want from the board Thursday: approve the Dunmore lease and the build-out budget
rubric: The ask (approve the Dunmore lease and build-out budget) is stated early in the deck or the opening, not held back until the last slide.
Slide titles say what the slide concludes, so a viewer reading only the titles in order could follow the argument, rather than topic labels like 'Overview' or 'Options'.
Option B is treated fairly: the answer shows that +26% falls short of the roughly 30% needed, using the supplied figures, instead of dismissing it.
Every number comes from the supplied facts or is plain arithmetic on them; no invented payback period, return, savings or market data.
The deck fits 15 minutes (roughly a dozen slides or fewer), with each slide carrying one idea, and what to say aloud is kept separate from what is on the slide.
Terms or context a non-food board member would need (what a commissary kitchen is, what utilization means) are made clear without a lecture.

prompt:
My team told me my sprint review deck is 'a lot'. I present it to the whole product group (about 40 people, in a room with a big screen) on Monday. Here are the slides as they stand. What would you change?

Slide 1: Q3 Sprint Review
- Team Harbor, Q3 sprints 14 through 19
- Presented by Imani Okafor, engineering manager

Slide 2: Overview
- Purpose of this review is to summarize work completed in sprints 14-19
- Cover velocity, shipped features, quality metrics, incidents, and the Q4 plan
- Questions welcome at end
- Appendix has additional detail

Slide 3: Velocity
- Sprint 14: 41 points; Sprint 15: 38; Sprint 16: 44; Sprint 17: 29 (two engineers out, holiday week); Sprint 18: 47; Sprint 19: 52
- Average over the quarter 41.8 points, up from 36.5 in Q2
- Commitment accuracy 84% (Q2 was 71%)
- Carry-over stories decreased from 9 to 4 per sprint on average

Slide 4: Shipped Features
- Saved filters on the shipment list
- CSV export now handles up to 50,000 rows
- New driver-assignment modal with conflict warnings
- Bulk edit for delivery windows
- Dark mode for the dispatcher console
- Role-based access for subcontractor accounts
- Rewrite of the notification service to use the new queue

Slide 5: Quality
- Escaped defects fell from 31 to 17
- Median time to fix a P2 bug dropped from 6.2 days to 3.5 days
- Test coverage on the dispatch module rose from 58% to 71%
- Two flaky end-to-end suites were removed and replaced with contract tests
- We still have no automated check for the CSV export path

Slide 6: Incident on Aug 29
- Notification queue backed up for 3 hours 10 minutes
- 1,140 delayed driver alerts
- Root cause: consumer config shipped with the notification rewrite had a prefetch limit set too low
- Fix deployed same day; alerting threshold on queue depth added the next week
- Follow-up: load test the queue before any future change

Slide 7: Q4 Plan
- Finish subcontractor permissions (phase 2)
- Start the route-optimization spike
- Pay down tech debt in the dispatch module
- Add the missing CSV export test
- Hire one senior engineer
- Investigate moving to a monthly release cadence

Slide 8: Thank You / Questions
rubric: Names specific slides and what is wrong or right on each, rather than only general advice to use fewer words.
Recognizes that the strong content (the improvements, the incident and its fix) is worth keeping, and points out the slides whose content is topic lists or logistics that add little for the audience.
Says what in the dense slides should move to speaker talking points or a handout and what should stay on screen, with a concrete example for at least one slide.
Suggests a clearer through-line for the deck, such as leading with the quarter's result, or making the incident and the Q4 decision stand out, instead of only trimming bullets.
Shows at least one rewritten slide (title and body) that is shorter and says something, using the facts given and no invented figures.

prompt:
I'm sending this to the volunteer leads tonight and presenting it at their meeting tomorrow morning (10 minutes, in the church hall with a projector). It's six slides. Can you give it a once-over before I send it? Here are the slides and my notes:

1. Title: 'Saturday distribution needs 9 more volunteers by March'
   On the slide: one line, 'We have 31 regulars. We need 40 for the new second line.'
   Notes: Open with the line count. Mention that the second line cuts the wait from about 50 minutes to about 25.

2. Title: 'The wait is the reason families leave without food'
   On the slide: a simple bar of wait times by hour (8am: 12 min, 9am: 31, 10am: 48, 11am: 52), labeled directly, with the 11am bar highlighted.
   Notes: 7 percent of arrivals in the last two months left before being served; most of them at 10 and 11.

3. Title: 'A second line at the east door fixes it, and costs no money'
   On the slide: a small floor-plan sketch with the new line marked.
   Notes: The church already approved the east door and the extra tables.

4. Title: 'The 9 shifts we need to fill are 10am to 1pm'
   On the slide: the three roles (check-in, bagging, carry-out) with the number needed for each: 3, 4, 2.
   Notes: Say that we will train on the first Saturday and no one has to lift heavy boxes unless they choose to.

5. Title: 'Pick a role today, and your first shift is March 4'
   On the slide: a sign-up QR code and the three roles.
   Notes: Pass the clipboard as well for anyone without a phone.

6. Title: 'Thank you'
   On the slide: the pantry logo and the phone number.
   Notes: Close by thanking the 31 who already show up.
rubric: Gives a clear overall verdict that the deck is already in good shape and says why, in specifics, rather than finding faults to look thorough.
Leaves the structure alone: does not propose adding slides, adding bullet text, a long agenda or an overview, or reordering the argument without a concrete reason.
Any changes proposed are few (at most about three), small and specific, and each says what to change and why.
Does not rewrite the deck; at most it offers a line or two of replacement wording for something it flags.
Does not invent problems or facts, and keeps the reply short enough to be a once-over.

prompt:
Our investment committee wants the Q3 update for the farmland fund emailed to them Friday. They'll go through it on their own over the weekend, and nobody will be presenting it, there's no meeting. They're all very familiar with the fund. Can you draft the slides? Facts:

- Orchard Ridge Farmland Fund holds 4,200 acres across three counties (Marlow, Teague, Cobb)
- 91% of acres are leased; the rest is between tenants and being marketed
- Average lease rate up 4.1% year over year
- Appraisal-based value per unit: $1,286 now vs $1,241 last quarter (+3.6%)
- Distribution paid this quarter: $18 per unit
- Two parcels in Marlow County, 310 acres in total, have drainage problems that cost the tenant part of last season's yield; repair estimate is $145,000
- Decision needed from the committee by Oct 31: approve the $145,000 drainage repair
- If the repair is not approved, the tenant has said they'll not renew those parcels in the spring
rubric: Each slide can be understood on its own without a presenter: it carries the full context and the supporting numbers and labels, not just a few words that only make sense when spoken over.
The decision needed (approve the $145,000 repair by Oct 31) and its consequence if not approved are prominent and early, not buried at the end.
Does not shrink the content to sparse slogans or a big number per slide; the density suits something read at a desk, while still being organized and scannable.
Does not rely on speaker notes to carry necessary content, because nobody is presenting.
Every figure comes from the supplied facts or is plain arithmetic on them; no invented projections, comparisons or benchmarks.

prompt: I'm giving a 20 minute talk to a regional meeting of dental hygienists about why patients tell us they floss when they don't. I'm stuck on the first line. Just give me one opening, a sentence or two, nothing else.
rubric: Gives exactly one opening of no more than about three sentences; does not offer a menu of options, an outline, speaker notes or a list of tips.
Does not state a statistic, study or survey result as fact, since none was supplied.

Is spoken-sounding and aimed at these listeners (people who ask patients this question every day), using a concrete moment or question they will recognize, not a generic greeting or an announcement of the topic.
Contains no preamble, explanation of its choice, or closing offer to refine; the reply is the opening.

prompt:
I get 3 minutes at the city council meeting on Tuesday to ask them to approve a protected bike lane on Alder Street. I've got three ways to start and I can't decide. Which one should I use, and why? I'll pick one and go with it.

A: 'Good evening, council members. My name is Dana Ortega, I'm with Cedar Hill Neighbors for Safe Streets, and tonight I'd like to walk you through our proposal for a protected bike lane on Alder Street between 4th and 12th.'

B: 'Last October a nine-year-old was clipped by a delivery van on Alder Street on her way to school. She's fine. The street she was crossing is the one I'm asking you to change tonight.'

C: 'Cities across the country have shown that protected cycling infrastructure reduces traffic injuries and increases foot traffic for local businesses, and Alder Street is an ideal candidate.'
rubric: Commits to a single recommended opening, stated early, rather than blending all three or declining to choose.
Gives reasons based on this situation (a 3-minute slot, an audience of council members hearing many speakers) and not generic taste.
Says specifically what is weak in each of the other two options.
Flags what the speaker must handle with the chosen opening, for example that the story is accurate and the family is comfortable with it being told, or how quickly the ask must follow.
Stays brief; does not rewrite the whole 3-minute speech.

prompt:
Make slide 9 for my quarterly ops review as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets), 16:9, built to fill a 1280x720 frame. It'll be projected in a conference room for the leadership team.

The point: our open support backlog fell from 412 tickets in March to 96 in September after we started the triage rotation in April.

The three things we changed:
- Tickets are sorted twice a day instead of weekly
- Billing questions go to a dedicated pair of people
- Anything older than 5 days gets an owner by name

Company is Brightwell Tools. Keep the style clean and neutral.
rubric: The slide's headline states the result (the backlog fell and by how much or from what to what), not a topic label like 'Support Backlog'.
The two key numbers, 412 and 96, are the largest elements and their relationship (before and after) is visible at a glance.
The three changes appear as short phrases that are clearly secondary to the result, and nothing else competes for attention.
Text is large enough to read from the back of a conference room, with strong contrast, and the whole slide fits the 16:9 frame without scrolling or cut-off.
Does not invent data: no chart with made-up monthly values between March and September, no extra statistics, no decorative filler.
Looks like a finished slide: aligned, with consistent spacing and a restrained palette.

prompt:
I had 30 minutes with the executive committee to review the patient portal rollout, and just found out I only get 10. I have 26 slides. Which ones should I keep, and in what order? The committee already knows the project exists; what they need from me is whether to fund phase 2. Here are my slides:

1. Title
2. Agenda
3. Who's on the project team
4. Why we started (2023 background)
5. Vendor selection process
6. Architecture diagram
7. Rollout timeline since 2023
8. Adoption by clinic (all 14 clinics, table)
9. Adoption: top 3 vs bottom 3 clinics
10. Monthly active patients, trend
11. Message volume by type
12. Front-desk call volume before and after
13. Staff time saved (estimate and method)
14. Patient satisfaction scores
15. Patient quotes
16. Three problems we hit
17. How we fixed login failures
18. Security and privacy review results
19. Cost to date vs budget
20. Phase 2 scope
21. Phase 2 cost and timeline
22. Risks if we don't fund phase 2
23. Alternatives we considered
24. Roadmap beyond phase 2
25. The ask: approve phase 2 funding
26. Thank you / questions
rubric: Provides a specific keep list, by slide number or title, that fits 10 minutes (on the order of 6 to 10 slides) and a clear order for it.
The keep list is built around the decision the committee has to make, and the ask is brought forward or made unmistakable rather than left as the final slide only.
Says what happens to the slides that are cut, such as moving them to an appendix or leaving them to the Q&A, and names a few that should be held back for questions.

Explains the reasoning for the major cuts and merges, such as dropping the agenda, introductions and background for an audience that already knows the project, rather than shaving a little off every section.
States what is lost or at risk with this cut, or what one question the committee is likely to ask that the appendix should cover.

prompt: I never know what to put on a slide versus what to just say out loud versus what goes in a handout. I'm presenting a forklift near-miss audit to the plant managers next week. Can you explain how to decide, using this one as the example? What I have: we reviewed 6 weeks of logs and camera footage, found 38 near-misses, 23 of them at the dock 6 crossing, 9 at the freezer door, and 6 scattered. Most happened between 2 and 4 pm, which is when the second shift handover overlaps with the peak of inbound trucks. We recommend a one-way rule and a stop line at dock 6, mirrors at the freezer door, and a staggered handover. I also have the full incident log, a list of every camera angle I reviewed, and the method I used to count a near-miss.
rubric: Gives a usable way to decide what belongs on the screen, what is spoken, and what goes in a handout, not just a description of the three places.

Applies it to this audit with concrete placement: for example which finding or number goes on a slide, what is said aloud, and that the full log, the camera list and the counting method go in the handout.
Uses only the supplied facts (38, 23, 9, 6, the 2 to 4 pm window, the recommendations); no invented statistics or incidents.
Addresses the audience of plant managers by saying what they will need to decide or do, and how that shapes what to show.
Is compact and organized; does not turn into a full deck or script.

prompt:
I need a 5-minute presentation for the product leadership meeting on Wednesday, built from our customer interviews. My VP wants the headline to say hardware store owners 'overwhelmingly' want online restock ordering, and she'd like a percentage on the slide. Make it land, they have to approve the build. Here's the data:

- 14 interviews with owners of independent hardware stores, done in September
- 9 said they would use online restock ordering if it connected to their register system
- 3 said maybe, depends on price
- 2 said no, they prefer calling their rep
- 5 mentioned that their current distributor's ordering portal is slow or confusing
- All 14 were recruited from our own customer newsletter list
- The request to leadership: approve a 10-week build of a restock ordering feature with register integration
rubric: Does not use 'overwhelmingly' or any wording that claims market-wide demand; the headline matches what 14 interviews support.
Any percentage shown is attached to the 14 interviewees (for example 9 of 14); it is not presented as a share of hardware store owners generally.
Mentions the limits somewhere visible, such as the small sample and that everyone came from the company's own newsletter list, without burying the finding.
Still makes the case: a clear structure, with slide titles that say what each slide concludes, the finding supported by the 9, 3, 2 and the portal complaints, and the build request stated.
Fits 5 minutes (about 4 to 7 slides) and uses only the supplied facts, with no invented quotes, revenue or market-size numbers.
